- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.7) and forecast shows a sharp downward move, reduce the magnitude of the drop to avoid overcorrection.  
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤-0.7) and forecast shows a sharp upward move, cap the upside to prevent overshoot.  
- If recent history shows a strong peak followed by a steep decline, model tends to overcorrect downward — adjust forecast to allow for a slower, more gradual decline.  
- If sentiment is mixed or neutral (±0.3) and forecast is trending sharply, reduce forecast volatility to match mean reversion tendencies.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome is consistently below forecast, especially after a spike, apply a downward bias correction by 5–10% of the forecasted range.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative sentiment spikes followed by recovery, model tends to overreact — dampen forecast recovery slope.  
- When sentiment is positive but recent prices are falling, model often overestimates the fall — adjust forecast to reflect a more moderate decline.  
- If forecast is consistently above true outcome and sentiment is neutral or slightly positive, reduce forecast by 3–5% to align with mean reversion.  
- For horizon > 14 days, if sentiment is positive and forecast is falling, consider a slight upward bias to avoid premature correction.
